hops.title: The epilepsy experiment that found a wave of silence
hops.text: In 1943 graduate student Aristides Leão stimulated rabbit cortex for an epilepsy thesis and got the opposite of a seizure: electrical activity nearly vanished, and the silence spread across the cortex at a few millimeters per minute, now called spreading depression. Later experiments found extracellular potassium reaching about 60 millimolar during the wave, roughly six times the ceiling this section gives for stimulated cat cortex, and depolarization that deep and lasting can stop neurons firing. In 1941 Karl Lashley had timed his migraine auras and estimated a wave crossing visual cortex at about 3 millimeters per minute. Functional MRI later tracked a similarly slow wave during human aura.

sources.citation: Costa C et al. (2013). Cortical spreading depression as a target for anti-migraine agents. The Journal of Headache and Pain 14:62.
Hadjikhani N et al. (2001). Mechanisms of migraine aura revealed by functional MRI in human visual cortex. PNAS 98(8):4687-4692.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A 1940s desk with a pencil sketch of a shimmering crescent, a stopwatch, and a chart recorder tracing a line that goes flat.
image.caption: During spreading depression, extracellular potassium surges and cortical activity falls quiet in a slow, traveling wave.

hops.title: One potassium channel, three organs: EAST or SeSAME syndrome
hops.text: Why would mutations in a single gene give one child seizures, unsteady balance, deafness and kidneys that waste salt? In 2009 two clinical teams found the answer in a rare inherited condition now called EAST or SeSAME syndrome: every affected child carried loss-of-function mutations in both copies of KCNJ10, the gene for Kir4.1. The channel behind spatial buffering has other jobs. In the brain, glia are believed to use it to take up the potassium that firing neurons release. In the inner ear it helps make the potassium-rich fluid that hearing depends on, and in the kidney it may recycle potassium, helping the sodium-potassium pump sustain salt reabsorption.

sources.citation: Bockenhauer D et al. (2009). Epilepsy, ataxia, sensorineural deafness, tubulopathy, and KCNJ10 mutations. New England Journal of Medicine 360(19):1960-1970.
Scholl UI et al. (2009). Seizures, sensorineural deafness, ataxia, mental retardation, and electrolyte imbalance (SeSAME syndrome) caused by mutations in KCNJ10. PNAS 106(14):5842-5847.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A carved spiral seashell, a jar of sea salt and a walnut side by side on a sunlit wooden shelf.
image.caption: One potassium channel, Kir4.1, serves brain glia, the inner ear and the kidney, so losing it affects all three.

hops.afterHeading: The axon's other partners: myelin, fuel and microglia
hops.title: Why a stubbed toe hurts twice
hops.text: If you have ever stubbed a bare toe on a table leg, you may have noticed that the pain arrives in two installments: a sharp, pinpoint jolt, then, after a pause, a dull ache that spreads. One knock started both. The jolt travels on thin, lightly myelinated axons at roughly 10 meters per second. The ache travels on unmyelinated pain axons, many of them bundled inside Remak cells, at roughly 1 meter per second. At those speeds, over about a meter of nerve, the two signals would reach the spinal cord roughly nine-tenths of a second apart, long enough for the ache to feel like a separate event.

sources.citation: Basbaum AI, Bautista DM, Scherrer G, Julius D (2009). Cellular and molecular mechanisms of pain. Cell 139(2):267-284.
Beissner F et al. (2010). Quick discrimination of A(delta) and C fiber mediated pain based on three verbal descriptors. PLoS ONE 5(9):e12944.
Harty BL, Monk KR (2017). Unwrapping the unappreciated: recent progress in Remak Schwann cell biology. Current Opinion in Neurobiology 47:131-137.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A young adult in striped socks sitting on a rug beside a table leg, holding one foot and wincing.
image.caption: A stubbed toe hurts twice: myelinated axons bring the sharp jolt, unmyelinated axons in Remak cells the ache.

audio.title: A silent wave, a fast shrimp and marathon myelin
audio.transcript:
This lesson treats the space around neurons, and the glia that tend it, as quiet plumbing. Here are three places where that plumbing stops being quiet: a rabbit brain that went silent, a shrimp with very fast nerves, and ten marathon runners.

First, the silent brain. In the early nineteen forties, a graduate student named Aristides Leão was studying experimental epilepsy in rabbits for his doctoral thesis. He stimulated the cortex, expecting the electrical storm of a seizure. Instead, the electrical activity on his recording nearly disappeared, one patch of cortex at a time, as a wave moved a few millimeters per minute. He published the finding in nineteen forty-four, and we now call it cortical spreading depression. In later experiments, potassium outside the cells reached about sixty millimolar during the wave. That is about six times the level reached when researchers strongly stimulated cat cortex in the experiment from this lesson. Depolarization that large and sustained can stop neurons firing altogether. The story has an odd prequel. In nineteen forty-one, the psychologist Karl Lashley had used his own migraines as an experiment, sketching the shimmering blind spot as it grew. From its spread he estimated that some wave was crossing his visual cortex at about three millimeters per minute. In two thousand one, a team used functional M R I to scan visual aura in three people with migraine. In one person they tracked a wave of signal change across visual cortex at about three and a half millimeters per minute. Its features matched spreading depression. A rabbit experiment and a psychologist's pencil sketches had probably been describing the same event.

Second, the shrimp. Myelin is usually taught as a vertebrate feature, made by Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes. But penaeid shrimp, the kind on a seafood platter, wrap their giant nerve fibers in compact, multilayered myelin. Their sheaths have regularly spaced openings called fenestration nodes, where the impulse jumps from one to the next, and an unusually wide space between the axon and the myelin. Researchers measured impulses in these fibers at more than two hundred meters per second, among the fastest nerve conduction recorded in any animal.

Third, the runners. This lesson's evidence says oligodendrocytes help fuel axons. A twenty twenty-five study asked whether myelin itself might be a fuel. Researchers scanned ten marathon runners with M R I in the two days before a race and again one to two days after, estimating the fraction of the water signal that came from between the layers of myelin. After the race, that fraction had fallen in twelve white matter regions, by as much as twenty-eight percent in one brainstem pathway and twenty-six percent in the corticospinal tract, a major motor pathway. The scans detected no clear change in brain volume or in water content in those regions. Two months later, the average in the six runners scanned again was back near pre-race levels. The authors suggest that when glycogen runs low over twenty-six miles, the brain may draw on myelin lipids for energy and rebuild them afterward. That is still a hypothesis. The runners' scans could not tell whether their brains actually burned myelin lipids for energy.

A slow wave that quiets the cortex, some of the fastest nerve signals ever recorded, and myelin that might serve as a fuel reserve: the cells that wrap and tend neurons do far more than hold them in place.
